props.title: In the Name of the Father
props.initialSlug: Wrongly jailed father and son fight for justice

sections.content: In the Name of the Father stands as one of cinema's most powerful examinations of wrongful imprisonment and judicial corruption. Jim Sheridan directs Daniel Day-Lewis in a tour-de-force performance as Gerry Conlon, wrongfully convicted as part of the Guildford Four for an IRA bombing. The film's raw power comes from the father-son relationship between Gerry and Giuseppe Conlon (Pete Postlethwaite), forced to share a prison cell while fighting to prove their innocence. Like The Hurricane (1999) and Just Mercy (2019), it exposes how justice systems can be weaponized against marginalized groups.

sections.content: The film sits within a crucial wave of 1990s Irish cinema that confronted The Troubles head-on. While Michael Collins (1996) tackled the birth of the IRA and The Crying Game (1992) explored identity and loyalty during the conflict, In the Name of the Father focused on the human cost of anti-Irish prejudice in Britain. Sheridan's direction keeps the political context clear while maintaining an intimate focus on the Conlon family's devastating journey.

The prison sequences reveal Sheridan's masterful control of claustrophobic space, reminiscent of A Prophet (2009) and Midnight Express (1978). Day-Lewis and Postlethwaite create an unforgettable portrait of a father and son discovering love and respect in the worst possible circumstances. Emma Thompson's portrayal of lawyer Gareth Peirce provides the film's moral center, showing how dedicated individuals can fight systemic injustice. SUBHEAD: Impact on Political Cinema

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond Irish cinema, setting a template for political dramas that balance personal stories with systemic critique. Erin Brockovich (2000) and Dark Waters (2019) follow similar structures, using individual cases to expose institutional corruption. The documentary-like approach to recreating historical events influenced later films like Bloody Sunday (2002) and '71 (2014), which also examine The Troubles from different perspectives.
